candidate.headline: You can agree to too much when someone else wants a bigger night.
candidate.body: Notice when someone keeps adding to an invitation, and accept only the part you can afford in time and money. Within ten minutes, they add drinks, another stop, and a shared tab you never budgeted for. You may feel stingy for keeping the original plan. One yes is enough. You are not rejecting them when you keep dinner to dinner.

candidate.headline: Someone else's enthusiasm makes too much seem reasonable.
candidate.body: Notice when you reconsider the plan because another person wants to add more, then repeat that dinner was the only thing you agreed to. You are reaching for your card to cover another round and checking if you can fit brunch into the free morning you meant to keep. You may feel ungenerous when they ask one more time. You were clear. Their disappointment does not make the additions your responsibility.

candidate.headline: They keep asking for more after you say yes.
candidate.body: Watch for the moment a quick dinner becomes drinks and another stop, then keep the end time you first agreed to. They order another round and ask you to stay out longer because the night is going well. You have an early start, and each added stop costs you sleep. You may feel stingy for leaving while they are still having fun. You are not spoiling the night. Their wish for more does not change the time you agreed to give.

candidate.headline: Their bigger plan starts taking over your evening.
candidate.body: Watch for the moment you agree to dinner and someone adds one more stop, another round, and a favor on the way home. You may feel difficult for objecting after you already said yes to the first plan. That is a new ask. Name the part you agreed to, decline the additions, and leave the larger plan with them. Your first yes does not cover every extra they add.
